explanation_text: Let A be the area of the parallel plate capacitor and d be the distance between the plates. Let [latex]C_1[/latex] be the capacitance of half portion with air as dielectic medium and [latex]C_2[/latex] be capacitance with a dielectic of permitivity, [latex]\varepsilon _r[/latex]. Then, [latex]C_1=\frac{\varepsilon _0 \left ( \frac{A}{2} \right )}{d}[/latex] (As area become half) and [latex]C_2=\frac{\varepsilon _0 \varepsilon _r \left ( \frac{A}{2} \right )}{d}[/latex] (As area becomes half) Now, these two capacitance will be in parallel if a voltage is applied between the plates as same potential difference will be there between both the capacitance. Equivalent capacitance is [latex]\begin{aligned} C_{eqv} &= C_1+C_2\\ &=\frac{\varepsilon _0 A}{2d}+ \frac{\varepsilon _0 \varepsilon _r A}{2d}\\ &= \frac{\varepsilon _0 A}{2d}(1+ \varepsilon _r)=\frac{C_0}{2}(1+\varepsilon _r) \end{aligned}[/latex] Therefore, modified capacitance, [latex]C_{eqv}=\frac{C_0}{2}(1+\varepsilon _r)[/latex]

[latex]C_{eqv}=\frac{C_0}{2}(1+\varepsilon _r)[/latex]

html: The core loss of a single phase, 230/115 V, 50 Hz power transformer is measured from 230 V side by feeding the primary (230 V side) from a variable voltage variable frequency source while keeping the secondary open circuited. The core loss is measured to be 1050 W for 230 V, 50 Hz input. The core loss is again measured to be 500 W for 138 V, 30 Hz input. The hysteresis and eddy current losses of the transformer for 230 V, 50 Hz input are respectively,
subject: Electrical Machines - Transformers
explanation_text: Given, at 230V, 50 Hz, core loss =1050 W and at 138 V, 30 Hz, core loss =500 W Let, [latex]V_1=230 V, \;f_1=50Hz[/latex] [latex]\begin{aligned} \text{Eddy current loss} &=P_{e1} \\ \text{Hysteresis loss}&=P_{h1} \\ V_2=138V &, f_230Hz \\ \text{Eddy current loss} &=P_{e2} \\ \text{Hysteresis loss}&=P_{h2} \\ \text{we know that, } & \\ \text{Eddy current loss,}\;& P_e \propto B_m^2f^2 \\ \text{and hysteresis loss,}&P_h \propto B_m^xf\propto B_m^1.6 f \\ &(\text{Typical value of x=1.6}) \end{aligned}[/latex] The transformer induced emf equation is: [latex]\begin{aligned} V_1 &=\sqrt{2} \pi \phi _m N \\ V_1&= \sqrt{2} \pi f B_m A N\\ \text{where,}\;\; \frac{V}{t} &=\text{constant} \end{aligned}[/latex] i.e. flux = constant ( to avoid over fluxing) [latex]\begin{aligned} \text{Eddy current loss,} &P_e \propto V^2 \\ \text{and hysteresis loss,}&P_h \propto\frac{V^{1.6}}{f^{0.6}} \end{aligned}[/latex] [latex]\begin{aligned} \frac{P_{e2}}{P_{e1}} &=\left ( \frac{V_2}{V_1} \right )^2=\left ( \frac{138}{230} \right )^2=0.36 \\ \text{or,} \;\; P_{e2} &= 0.36P_{e1}\;\;...(i)\\ \text{Also,} \;\;\frac{P_{h2}}{P_{e1}} &=\left ( \frac{V_2}{V_1} \right )^{1.6} \times \left ( \frac{f_1}{f_2} \right )^{0.6}\\ &=\left ( \frac{138}{230} \right )^{1.6} \times \left ( \frac{50}{30} \right )^{0.6} \\ &= (0.6)^{1.6} \times \frac{1}{(0.6)^{0.6}}=0.6\\ \therefore \;\; P_{h2} &=0.6P_{h1} \;\;...(ii) \end{aligned} [/latex] Given at 230V, 50Hz [latex]\text{Core loss}=P_{e1}+P_{h1}=1050W\;\;...(iii) [/latex] At 138V, 30Hz, [latex]\text{Core loss}=P_{e2}+P_{h2}=500W [/latex] or,   [latex]0.36P_{e1}+0.6P_{h1}=500W\;\;...(iv)[/latex] solving equation (iii) and (iv), we get [latex]P_{h1}=508W [/latex] and [latex] P_{e1}=542W[/latex] Therefore, hysteresis and eddy current losses at 230V, 50Hz are 508W and 542W respectively.
explanation_html:
Given, at 230V, 50 Hz, core loss =1050 W
and at 138 V, 30 Hz, core loss =500 W
Let, [latex]V_1=230 V, \;f_1=50Hz[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} \text{Eddy current loss} &=P_{e1} \\ \text{Hysteresis loss}&=P_{h1} \\ V_2=138V &, f_230Hz \\ \text{Eddy current loss} &=P_{e2} \\ \text{Hysteresis loss}&=P_{h2} \\ \text{we know that, } & \\ \text{Eddy current loss,}\;& P_e \propto B_m^2f^2 \\ \text{and hysteresis loss,}&P_h \propto B_m^xf\propto B_m^1.6 f \\ &(\text{Typical value of x=1.6}) \end{aligned}[/latex]
The transformer induced emf equation is:
[latex]\begin{aligned} V_1 &=\sqrt{2} \pi \phi _m N \\ V_1&= \sqrt{2} \pi f B_m A N\\ \text{where,}\;\; \frac{V}{t} &=\text{constant} \end{aligned}[/latex]
i.e. flux = constant ( to avoid over fluxing)
[latex]\begin{aligned} \text{Eddy current loss,} &P_e \propto V^2 \\ \text{and hysteresis loss,}&P_h \propto\frac{V^{1.6}}{f^{0.6}} \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} \frac{P_{e2}}{P_{e1}} &=\left ( \frac{V_2}{V_1} \right )^2=\left ( \frac{138}{230} \right )^2=0.36 \\ \text{or,} \;\; P_{e2} &= 0.36P_{e1}\;\;...(i)\\ \text{Also,} \;\;\frac{P_{h2}}{P_{e1}} &=\left ( \frac{V_2}{V_1} \right )^{1.6} \times \left ( \frac{f_1}{f_2} \right )^{0.6}\\ &=\left ( \frac{138}{230} \right )^{1.6} \times \left ( \frac{50}{30} \right )^{0.6} \\ &= (0.6)^{1.6} \times \frac{1}{(0.6)^{0.6}}=0.6\\ \therefore \;\; P_{h2} &=0.6P_{h1} \;\;...(ii) \end{aligned} [/latex]
Given at 230V, 50Hz
[latex]\text{Core loss}=P_{e1}+P_{h1}=1050W\;\;...(iii) [/latex]
At 138V, 30Hz,
[latex]\text{Core loss}=P_{e2}+P_{h2}=500W [/latex]
or, [latex]0.36P_{e1}+0.6P_{h1}=500W\;\;...(iv)[/latex]
solving equation (iii) and (iv), we get
[latex]P_{h1}=508W [/latex] and [latex] P_{e1}=542W[/latex]
Therefore, hysteresis and eddy current losses at 230V, 50Hz are 508W and 542W respectively.

[latex]\;\; \;\;=230-4 \times 0.4=228.4 V [/latex]
Also, at full load,
[latex]I_{L_{fl}}=70A [/latex]
[latex]I_{a_{fl}}=I_{L_{fl}}-I_f=70-1=69A [/latex]
Induced emf at full load,
[latex]E_{a_{fl}}=V-I_{a{fl}}R_a [/latex]
[latex]E_{a_{fl}}=230 -69 \times 0.4=202.4V [/latex]
we know that,

&\text{Solvinf eq. (i) and (ii), we have}\\

&\text{Contribution of }S_1 \text{in 100 A at location}\\
P&=I_1-200=0A \\
&\text{Contribution of }S_2 \text{in 100 A at location}\\

subject: Electrical and Electronic Measurements - Galvanometers, Voltmeters and Ammeters
explanation_text: For a PMMC ammeter, at equilibrim, we have : controlling torque ([latex]T_c[/latex])=Deflecting torque([latex]T_d[/latex]) [latex]\begin{aligned} K\theta _1 &=GI \; \text{or}\; \theta _1=\frac{GI}{K}\\ where, \;\; G &= nBA\\ \therefore \; \theta _1 &= \frac{nBAI}{K} \end{aligned}[/latex] For an electrodynometer ammeter, at equilibrium, Controlling torque=Deflecting torque [latex]\begin{aligned} i.e. \;\; T_c &=T_d \; \text{or}\; K \theta _2=I^2 \frac{dM}{d\theta }\\ or, \;\; \theta _2 &= \frac{I^2}{K}\cdot \frac{dM}{d\theta }\;\;...(ii)\\ \end{aligned}[/latex] For the deflection in the two meter to be same, [latex]\begin{aligned} \theta _1 &=\theta _2\\ or, \;\; \frac{nBAI}{K} &= \frac{I^2}{K}\cdot \frac{dM}{d\theta }\\ or, \;\; nBA&=I\frac{dM}{d\theta }\\ or, \;\; I &=\frac{nBA}{\left ( \frac{dM}{d\theta } \right )} \end{aligned}[/latex] [latex]\begin{aligned} Given, \;\; n&= \text{number of turns}=100\\ B&= 0.2 Wb/m^2\\ A&=80mm^2=80 \times 10^{-6}m^2\\ \text{and}\;\; \frac{dM}{d\theta }&=0.5 mH/rad\\ &=0.5 \times 10^{-3}H/rad \\ \end{aligned}[/latex] Putting the values in I, we get [latex]\begin{aligned} I &=\left ( \frac{100 \times 0.2 \times 80 \times 10^{-6}}{0.5 \times 10^{-3}} \right ) A\\ &= \frac{1.6}{0.5}=3.2A \end{aligned} [/latex] [latex]\therefore[/latex]  Required value of current, [latex]I=3.2Amp.[/latex]
explanation_html:
For a PMMC ammeter, at equilibrim, we have :
controlling torque ([latex]T_c[/latex])=Deflecting torque([latex]T_d[/latex])
[latex]\begin{aligned} K\theta _1 &=GI \; \text{or}\; \theta _1=\frac{GI}{K}\\ where, \;\; G &= nBA\\ \therefore \; \theta _1 &= \frac{nBAI}{K} \end{aligned}[/latex]
For an electrodynometer ammeter, at equilibrium,
Controlling torque=Deflecting torque
[latex]\begin{aligned} i.e. \;\; T_c &=T_d \; \text{or}\; K \theta _2=I^2 \frac{dM}{d\theta }\\ or, \;\; \theta _2 &= \frac{I^2}{K}\cdot \frac{dM}{d\theta }\;\;...(ii)\\ \end{aligned}[/latex]
